usageSteps: Search for a city, airport, or landmark, or tap "Use my location" to check conditions right where you are. The airspace information and the regulation link you see depend on the country of the selected location.

Review live wind speed, wind gusts, visibility, and temperature, plus the wind at 10 m, 80 m, and 120 m above ground. Gusts matter more than the average wind speed, and wind is often stronger at higher altitude. The banner at the top combines the gust and the Kp index into one general reading: gusts under 5.6 m/s are good, 5.6 m/s up to 9.7 m/s call for caution, and 9.7 m/s or more is not recommended.

Check the planetary Kp index to see whether geomagnetic activity might affect your GPS lock or compass heading. A Kp below 4 is quiet, 4 up to 5 is unsettled, and 5 or higher is storm level, where GPS accuracy and compass reliability can drop.

Use the airspace card and the airspace layers on the map to see the restricted areas of the selected country, and confirm the latest rules with the official authority through the regulation button. In the US, see the FAA UAS Facility Map altitude ceiling for the area — then confirm authorization through LAANC or FAADroneZone before you fly.

Use the 24-Hour Flight Conditions forecast to find the best time window. Each hour is rated good, caution, or not recommended from the forecast gusts, precipitation (caution from 0.1 mm per hour, not recommended from 0.5 mm), and visibility (caution under 5 km, not recommended under 1 km). The summary above the cards shows the longest good stretch, in the local time of the selected location. The current reading and the forecast for the current hour may not match exactly, so small differences can appear. This rating does not include the Kp index, airspace rules, or night-flying regulations, so check those separately.

In "Wind Check for Your Drone", pick your drone model to compare the current gust with the manufacturer's official maximum wind speed. Below 50% of that figure is good, 50% or more calls for caution, and 70% or more is not recommended. Your choice is also applied to the 24-hour forecast and is stored only in this browser.

Treat every rating as a reference only. Aircraft condition, battery, payload, local rules, and night-flying requirements are not included, so the final decision and responsibility remain with the pilot. The guides on this site explain the thresholds and background in more detail.

faq.question: Is FlyDroneMap a substitute for FAA flight authorization?
faq.answer: No. The airspace ceiling shown here comes from the FAA's public UAS Facility Map data and is for planning reference only. You must still obtain authorization through LAANC or FAADroneZone where required before flying.

faq.question: Where does the weather data come from?
faq.answer: Wind speed, gusts, visibility, and temperature come from Open-Meteo's public weather API, updated frequently throughout the day.

faq.question: What is the Kp index and why does it matter for drone flights?
faq.answer: The planetary Kp index measures geomagnetic activity. During elevated Kp levels (geomagnetic storms), GPS positioning accuracy and compass readings can be less reliable, which matters for drones that rely on GPS-hold or return-to-home.

faq.question: Does FlyDroneMap work outside the United States?
faq.answer: Wind, visibility, and Kp index data work worldwide. The FAA airspace ceiling feature is US-specific, since it's sourced from FAA data — outside the US it will show no data for that card.

faq.question: Do I need to create an account?
faq.answer: No. FlyDroneMap works without sign-up — just search a location and check the conditions.

faq.question: Is FlyDroneMap free to use?
faq.answer: Yes, completely free. The site is supported by ads and occasional affiliate links, which never affect the accuracy of the data shown.

Home.thresholdBasis: How the thresholds are set: gusts under 5.6 m/s show as good, 5.6–9.7 m/s as caution and 9.7 m/s or more as no-fly. These cut-offs are this site's own rule of thumb, chosen to stay below the 8–12.8 m/s maximum wind resistance that manufacturers list for common models — no authority publishes them. For a selected model, 50% of the manufacturer's figure is caution and 70% is not recommended, a conservative choice made by this site. Kp 4 shows as unsettled and Kp 5 or higher as storm: NOAA issues Kp alerts when Kp reaches 4 and rates Kp 5 as a G1 geomagnetic storm. The precipitation (0.1 / 0.5 mm) and visibility (5 / 1 km) cut-offs are also this site's own rules of thumb.

sections.heading: What is FlyDroneMap
body: FlyDroneMap is a free, no-signup dashboard for drone pilots. Search any location to see live wind speed, wind gusts, visibility, and the latest planetary Kp index, plus — for US locations — the FAA's public UAS Facility Map altitude ceiling.

sections.heading: Why We Built It
body: Checking flight conditions usually means piecing together several different apps and government sites. FlyDroneMap brings the numbers that actually matter for a go/no-go decision — wind, gusts, visibility, and geomagnetic activity — into one place, in your language.

sections.heading: Not a Substitute for Official Authorization
body: FlyDroneMap is a planning reference, not a flight authorization tool. Always confirm your flight through LAANC or FAADroneZone (in the US) or your local aviation authority before flying.

sections.heading: Where the data comes from
body: Weather data — wind, gusts, visibility and temperature — comes from Open-Meteo. The planetary Kp index comes from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC).

Airspace layers come from official public services: the FAA UAS Facility Map and airspace data for the United States, VWorld for South Korea, ENAIRE's UAS geographical zones for Spain, DIPUL for Germany, FOCA's drone map for Switzerland, and the DGAC restriction map for France. For Japan we currently link to the official MLIT pages only.

sections.heading: Accuracy, updates and corrections
body: Regulation summaries are short, plain-language references, not legal advice, and each country page links to the official authority. Rules change, so always confirm with the authority before you fly.

Every guide shows its publication date, and we aim to revise a guide when the rules or data it is based on change. If you spot an error or an outdated rule, email us and we will check it against the official source.

us.name: United States
summary: Recreational flyers must pass the online TRUST safety test, while commercial drone operations require an FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate.

Drones weighing 250 g (0.55 lb) or more must be registered with the FAA and broadcast Remote ID, and flying in controlled airspace near airports requires prior FAA authorization through LAANC or DroneZone.
Always check airspace with the B4UFLY app or the FAA's UAS facility map before you fly.
highlights: Recreational flyers must pass the free online TRUST safety test and carry proof of completion while flying.
Register any drone weighing 250 g (0.55 lb) or more. A registered drone must also broadcast Remote ID, unless it is flown inside an FAA-Recognized Identification Area (FRIA).
In uncontrolled (Class G) airspace, fly at or below 400 ft and keep the drone within visual line of sight, or use a visual observer who is next to you.
In Class B, C, D and surface Class E airspace near airports, you need prior FAA authorization, requested through LAANC or DroneZone.
Flying for work or business falls under Part 107 instead of the recreational rules: you need an FAA Remote Pilot Certificate, and the aircraft must weigh under 55 lb.
checklist: Carry your TRUST completion proof and put your FAA registration number on the drone.
Check the airspace in the B4UFLY app or the FAA's Where Can I Fly? resource before every flight.
Request LAANC authorization before you fly in controlled airspace near an airport.
Look for temporary flight restrictions (TFRs) and NOTAMs that cover your location and time.

kr.name: South Korea
kr.authority: Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport (MOLIT) · Drone OneStop
summary: Depending on weight and purpose, you must register your drone and obtain flight approval in advance through the Drone OneStop portal. For photos and video, use Drone OneStop's aerial-filming application (it replaced the old permit system in December 2022) to check whether prohibited-photography facilities, such as military or security facilities, lie in the filming area.

Flying in a place that needs permission without it can lead to fines or penalties under the Aviation Safety Act, and breaking the pilot conduct rules can bring a fine of up to KRW 2 million, according to Drone OneStop. Parts of central Seoul and areas near the armistice line are no-fly zones, and the surroundings of airfields (within 9.3 km) are control zones, so check the Drone OneStop map before every flight.
On this site, selecting a location in South Korea also shows no-fly zones, control zones, and other airspace layers in color on the map.
highlights: A multicopter with a maximum takeoff weight over 2 kg must be registered. Drones used in a business under the Aviation Business Act (aircraft rental, aviation leisure sports or ultralight-aircraft use business) are also subject to registration. Whether use counts as business depends on the actual purpose, so check Drone OneStop's registration FAQ if unsure.

Whether a pilot certificate is needed, and which class, may depend on factors such as the type and weight of the drone. Check the details yourself on the Korea Transportation Safety Authority (KOTSA) pilot certificate page.

Flying in the following places is restricted and needs permission from the regional aviation office or the Ministry of National Defense: within 9.3 km of an airfield (control zone), no-fly zones (near the armistice line and parts of central Seoul) and altitudes of 150 m or higher. Drones over 25 kg also need flight approval. According to Drone OneStop, a drone of 25 kg or less flown in daytime below 150 m outside control zones and no-fly zones does not need flight approval.

Flying at night (sunset to sunrise) or beyond the distance where you can see the drone with your own eyes needs a special flight approval from the regional aviation office. Special flight approval is separate from ordinary flight approval.

Pilot conduct rules apply to everyone regardless of weight or purpose (Aviation Safety Act Article 129): do not drop objects, do not fly in a dangerous way over crowds or densely populated areas, do not fly so close to buildings that you could collide, do not fly under the influence of alcohol, and do not fly when you cannot see the drone. Violations can bring a fine of up to KRW 2 million.
checklist: Check your drone's maximum takeoff weight and how you use it (business or not) against Drone OneStop's registration FAQ.
Check your location on the Drone OneStop map ('지도로 확인하기') and apply in advance for flight approval where it is needed.

For photos and video, use the aerial-filming application on Drone OneStop to check whether prohibited-photography facilities are in the filming area. Do not film military installations or other prohibited-photography facilities.
Fly in daylight, with the drone in sight, and keep away from crowds. For places such as parks, beaches, national parks or cultural heritage sites, consult the owner or manager beforehand.

jp.name: Japan
jp.authority: Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT)
summary: Drones weighing 100 g or more that are flown outdoors must be registered and equipped with Remote ID, as required by law.

Flying near airports, at 150 m or higher above ground, over event venues, or when transporting dangerous goods or dropping objects requires prior permission or approval, applied for online via DIPS 2.0 (submit at least 10 business days before the flight; 3–4 weeks ahead is recommended).

Flights over densely inhabited districts (DID), at night, or beyond visual line of sight are also special flights (Category II); a permit can be waived when the pilot holds the required skill certificate, the aircraft is certified, and a flight manual is in place. Always check the latest rules on the official site before flying.
highlights: Drones weighing 100 g or more that are flown outdoors must be registered. Registration is valid for 3 years.
You must display the registration ID on the aircraft and equip it with Remote ID.

Flights near airports and at 150 m or higher above the ground or water are generally prohibited unless you coordinate with the authority and get approval. Around eight major airports, flights under the approach and transitional surfaces and above the airport grounds are also generally prohibited.

Permission or approval is also needed for flights over densely inhabited districts (DID), at night, beyond visual line of sight, within 30 m of people or objects, over event sites, when carrying dangerous goods or when dropping objects. Flying without the proper permission or approval can lead to imprisonment (拘禁刑) or a fine.
Drones with a total weight of 25 kg or more need third-party liability insurance when they apply for new permission or approval on or after 1 October 2025.
checklist: Register the drone, display the registration ID and set up Remote ID before the first flight.
Check the surroundings of airports and densely inhabited districts (DID) on a map before you choose a flight location.
If your flight is a specific flight, apply through DIPS 2.0 at least 10 business days ahead, and allow 3 to 4 weeks in total.
Keep 30 m away from people and objects unless you have approval.

jp.metaDescription: Japan drone rules: drones of 100 g or more must be registered with MLIT (incl. Remote ID). Learn when permission is needed near airports and for night flights.

es.name: Spain
summary: Spain follows the EU-wide EASA framework, which splits drone operations into three risk-based categories — Open, Specific, and Certified. Most hobby flying falls under the Open category.

Operators must register with AESA if their drone weighs 250 g or more, or if a lighter drone has a camera or sensor that can capture personal data (unless it complies with the Toy Safety Directive). The operator registration number must be included on all of the operator's drones.
Geographical UAS zones are set by Royal Decree 517/2024. AESA points to the ENAIRE drone app to see where drone flights are prohibited or restricted — always check it before flying.
highlights: Spain applies the EU Open category to most hobby flights: a drone under 25 kg, flown within visual line of sight and at most 120 m above the ground, with no prior authorization.

You must register as an operator with AESA if the drone weighs 250 g or more, can transfer more than 80 joules of energy on impact, or has a camera or microphone (unless it complies with the Toy Safety Directive). Registration is done through AESA's electronic headquarters.

Pilots need the free online A1/A3 certificate (40 questions, 40 minutes, 75% to pass, valid for 5 years) for C1 drones (A1) and C2, C3 or C4 drones (A3). The A2 subcategory is limited to class C2 drones and also needs the A2 exam and declared practical self-training.

Class labels set the limits: C0 under 250 g, C1 under 900 g, C2 under 4 kg, and C3 and C4 under 25 kg. A drone placed on the market before 1 January 2024 without a class label needs no certificate if it is under 250 g (only familiarity with the manufacturer's manual), and the A3 certificate if it is 250 g or more.
Registration with AESA is valid across the EASA member states, but it does not authorize a flight anywhere: national airspace restrictions still apply.
checklist: Check your drone's class label (C0 to C4) and the subcategory it allows before you fly.
Put your operator registration number on every drone you fly.
Get the free AESA A1/A3 certificate if your drone requires it. AESA recommends it even where it is not mandatory.
Check ENAIRE's drone app for geographical UAS zones before every flight.

de.name: Germany
summary: Germany follows the EU-wide EASA framework, which splits drone operations into three risk-based categories — Open, Specific, and Certified. Most hobby flying falls under the Open category.

Operators must register with the LBA (Luftfahrt-Bundesamt) if their drone has a take-off mass of 250 g or more, or if a lighter drone has a sensor that captures personal data, such as a camera. The electronic registration number (e-ID) must be attached to each drone.

Before each flight, the LBA recommends checking the DIPUL platform's map tool for geographical UAS zones (federal zones are set out in § 21h of the German Air Traffic Regulation, LuftVO). DIPUL's map also shows zones in other EU countries, where rules can differ.
highlights: Register with the LBA if your drone has a take-off mass of 250 g or more, or if a lighter drone has a camera or other sensor that captures personal data (toys excluded). Registration applies to the operator, and the e-ID you receive must be attached to the drone.

From 250 g you need an EU competence certificate. The A1/A3 certificate comes from an online course and exam (40 questions, at least 75% correct). Subcategory A2 requires the A1/A3 certificate, an additional theory exam at an LBA-approved test centre and a class C2 drone.
Liability insurance is mandatory under § 43 of the Air Traffic Act (LuftVG). Flying without it is an administrative offence, and you must carry the insurance certificate.
In the Open category, the maximum flight altitude is 120 m above ground.
Drones under 250 g need no exam, but their operators must still know and follow the rules.
checklist: Check that your LBA registration is current and the e-ID is attached to the drone.
Make sure your liability insurance covers drone flights, and carry the insurance certificate.
Make sure you hold the competence certificate (A1/A3 or A2) that your drone requires. Drones under 250 g need no exam.
Check the DIPUL map for geographical zones before every flight, also in other EU countries where the rules can differ.

de.metaDescription: Germany drone rules under the EU EASA framework: Open, Specific and Certified categories, LBA registration, and how to check DIPUL flight restriction zones.

fr.name: France
fr.authority: DGAC (French Directorate General for Civil Aviation)
summary: France applies the EU drone framework (Implementing Regulation 2019/947) and adds national rules on top. The Open category covers low-risk operations, for leisure and professional use, and the DGAC itself advises checking the national specifics of every EU member state.

An operator must register on the AlphaTango portal before flying if the drone weighs more than 250 g, or if it is not a toy and carries a sensor that can collect personal data, such as a camera or a microphone. Remote pilots in subcategories A1/A3 complete training and a 40-question exam, A2 adds practical training and a 30-question exam, and the minimum age is 14.

In the Open category France prohibits night flights and flights in public space in built-up areas, and the maximum height is 120 m. Before each flight, check the DGAC restriction map for your location and the SIA website for temporary zones. The DGAC says the map has gaps, for example private helipads and temporary nesting-period bans.
highlights: Register as a European UAS operator on AlphaTango if your drone weighs more than 250 g, or if it is not a toy and carries a camera, microphone or other sensor that can collect personal data. After registration, the DGAC says open-category flying needs no declaration and no prior authorisation, but it must comply with the European regulations and the national orders.

For A1/A3 you complete training and pass a 40-question exam, and for A2 you add, after the A1/A3 theory, practical training and a 30-question exam, with 75 percent correct answers expected in both. The DGAC says the certificates are recognised in all EU member states. The minimum age in France is 14.

Flying over gatherings of people is never allowed in the Open category. In A2, overflight is prohibited and the DGAC lists 5 m from people in low-speed mode and 30 m otherwise. In A3, overflight is prohibited and the DGAC's table lists 150 m from people.

Night flights and flights in public space in built-up areas are prohibited in the Open category, and the maximum height is 120 m. The prefect can grant exceptions to the night ban, and the DGAC says the request must be sent at least 30 days before the flights.

Drones over 800 g must emit an electronic signal under French rules, with some stated exemptions. The 800 g figure is separate from the 250 g registration rule, and the DGAC's description of penalties for missing training or registration refers to drones of 800 g or more.
checklist: Register on AlphaTango if your drone is over 250 g or carries a camera or microphone, and make sure you hold the right certificate (A1/A3 or A2) and are at least 14.
Check the DGAC restriction map for the exact location before every flight, and the SIA website for temporary zones. The map does not show private helipads or temporary nesting-period bans.
Do not plan night flights, flights in public space in built-up areas or flights above 120 m in the Open category.

If you visit from abroad, read the DGAC's rules for visitors: EU operators need their EU registration, and operators from states outside EASA must register as European operators and obtain European qualifications.

ch.name: Switzerland
ch.authority: FOCA (Swiss Federal Office of Civil Aviation)
summary: Switzerland is not an EU member, but the Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA, BAZL in German) lists EU Implementing Regulation 2019/947 among the legislation behind its drone rules and says certificates and registrations are recognised across the EASA member states: the EU states, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. Flights without a FOCA authorisation must follow the open-category rules, and complex flights need a special-category authorisation.

Operators register with FOCA on the dLIS platform unless the drone weighs less than 250 g and has no camera or other sensor that can record personal data. Operators of drones over 250 g must give their insurance details when they register, and remote pilots need a certificate (A1/A3 or A2), except for class C0 drones and light legacy or privately built drones in A1.

Before every flight, FOCA requires pilots to check the drone map for national and cantonal restrictions and the Daily Airspace Bulletin Switzerland (DABS). A permit for a restricted area comes from the area's own competent body, not from FOCA.
highlights: Register as an operator on dLIS unless your drone is under 250 g and has no camera, microphone or other sensor for personal data. You need an eIAM account (AGOV or CH-Login). FOCA lists a minimum age of 12 for registration, with the name of a legal representative for children under 16, and the registration is valid for an unlimited period.

Show the first part of your UAS operator number (CHE plus 13 characters) clearly on every drone before each flight, and failing to do so is punishable. The last three characters are only used to activate Remote ID, and FOCA advises treating them like a password.
Operators of drones over 250 g must give their insurance details when they register. Before you fly, check with your insurer and on the FOCA website which liability cover your drone needs.

In every subcategory the maximum height is 120 m above ground, you must stay within line of sight, flying over crowds is prohibited, manned aviation has priority and Remote ID must be on. In A2 the distance to uninvolved people is the greater of 30 m (5 m in low-speed mode) and the flight height, and A3 requires 150 m from residential, commercial, industrial and recreational areas where 10 or more uninvolved people are within a 100 m radius.

Certificates are valid for five years in all EASA member states, and certificates from EASA states are valid in Switzerland while those from other states are not recognised. The minimum age is 12 in the open category (younger children only under the direct supervision of a person aged 16 or over) and 14 in the special category.
checklist: Check that your operator registration is in place, that every drone shows the visible part of your operator number, and that you have checked with your insurer which liability cover your drone needs.
Make sure you hold the certificate your flight requires (A1/A3 or A2) and can show it during the flight.
Before every flight, check the drone map, the current DABS and the areas with an increased collision risk, and request a permit from the competent body if a restriction applies.
Stay within line of sight and below 120 m, keep the distances of your subcategory and switch Remote ID on.

gb.name: United Kingdom
summary: In the United Kingdom, drone flying is overseen by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA). Most leisure flying and low-risk commercial flying falls under the Open category, and the CAA's Drone and Model Aircraft Code is the main reference for it.

Most outdoor flying requires a Flyer ID (you get it by passing the CAA's online theory test) and an Operator ID (which registers the person responsible for the aircraft). Which of them you need depends on the aircraft's weight or class mark and on whether it has a camera. The CAA does not recognise overseas registrations or qualifications, so visiting pilots need UK IDs before flying in the UK.

Before each flight, check the restrictions for your location. Most airports, airfields and spaceports have a Flight Restriction Zone (FRZ), and you must never fly in one without permission. The map of airspace restrictions published by NATS is one source to check, but the CAA notes that it does not show everything, especially restrictions created at short notice.
highlights: Flyer ID: required for aircraft weighing 100 g or more. You get it by passing the CAA's online theory test. There is no minimum age, but children under 13 must take the test and register with a parent or guardian. A Flyer ID lasts five years.

Operator ID: required for aircraft weighing 250 g or more, and for aircraft of 100 g or more that have a camera. It is optional for 100–250 g aircraft without a camera and not needed under 100 g. Registrants must be 18 or over, the ID is renewed every year, and it must be displayed on the aircraft.
Do not fly above 120 m (400 ft) above the closest point of the ground, and keep the aircraft in direct sight at all times with a full view of the surrounding airspace. Never fly over crowds.

Keep at least 50 m horizontally from people and do not fly over them, unless they are involved in your flight. Aircraft under 250 g, or with class mark UK0 or UK1, may fly closer to people and over them, but never over crowds. Other aircraft must also stay at least 150 m from residential, recreational, commercial and industrial areas.

Since 1 January 2026, UK1, UK2 and UK3 aircraft must have Remote ID added and switched on before flight. Never fly in the Flight Restriction Zone of an airport, airfield or spaceport without permission.
checklist: Check that your Flyer ID is valid, and that your Operator ID (not your Flyer ID) is displayed on every aircraft you fly.
Look up your aircraft's weight and class mark on the CAA's class marks page to confirm which rules apply.

Before every flight, check the NATS airspace restriction map and NOTAMs for Flight Restriction Zones and other restrictions, and remember that these sources may be incomplete. Also look out for restricted sites, temporary event bans and local byelaw signs.
If you fly at night, switch on a green flashing light. Insurance is optional for recreational flying under 20 kg but required for paid work and for aircraft of 20 kg or more.

ca.name: Canada
summary: In Canada, drones are regulated by Transport Canada under Part IX of the Canadian Aviation Regulations. The rules depend on the drone's weight: microdrones under 250 g have their own rules and need no registration or pilot certificate, while drones from 250 g up to 25 kg must be registered and flown by a certified pilot.

Drones are registered online through Transport Canada's Drone Management Portal, and the registration number must be marked on the drone. Basic operations require the Pilot Certificate – Basic Operations (passing the Small Basic online exam, minimum age 14). Flying closer to people or in controlled airspace requires the Advanced certificate (minimum age 16).

To plan where to fly, Transport Canada points to the NRC Drone Site Selection Tool, which shows prohibited, restricted and potentially hazardous areas, and to NAV Drone, which is used to request permission in NAV CANADA-controlled airspace. Foreign pilots and operators cannot register a drone in Canada and need a Special Flight Operations Certificate (SFOC-RPAS) to comply with the rules, so visitors should check Transport Canada's guidance before travelling.
highlights: Under 250 g (microdrones): no registration and no pilot certificate are required, but the other rules still apply, such as staying away from emergency sites and restricted airspace. The weight of anything attached, such as a camera or safety cage, counts; the remote controller does not.
From 250 g up to 25 kg: the drone must be registered with Transport Canada and marked with its registration number. Penalties apply for flying an unregistered or unmarked drone.

Basic operations need the Pilot Certificate – Basic Operations (Small Basic online exam, minimum age 14, the certificate does not expire). Carry the certificate and your proof of registration. The Advanced certificate (minimum age 16) is needed for operations such as flying in controlled airspace or closer to people.

To stay within basic operations, keep the drone in sight at all times, stay more than 30 m horizontally from any person, fly only in uncontrolled airspace, and stay more than 5.6 km (3 NM) from certified airports and more than 1.9 km (1 NM) from certified heliports. Within 5.6 km of a military aerodrome you need Department of National Defence permission.

Do not fly inside the security perimeter of an emergency response, or within 9.3 km (5 NM) of a wildfire. Takeoff and landing inside a national park are not permitted unless the park superintendent allows it. Flying near advertised outdoor events requires an SFOC, even for microdrones.
checklist: Confirm your drone's operating weight, including any camera or other attachment, to see whether registration and a pilot certificate apply.
Check that the drone is registered and marked, and carry your pilot certificate and proof of registration.
Survey the area and check the NRC Drone Site Selection Tool, NAV Drone and current NOTAMs before each flight. The NRC tool is a convenience tool only.
Insurance is not required for standard operations but is recommended. For altitude limits and the rules for foreign operators, check Transport Canada's pages before you fly.

au.name: Australia
summary: In Australia, drones are regulated by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA), and CASA's drone safety rules simplify the regulations in Part 101 of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations. Flying for fun does not require drone registration, a licence or operator accreditation, including for micro drones.

Flying for work or business is different: it requires drone registration, operator accreditation or a remote pilot licence, and compliance with the rules for that type of operation. CASA groups drones by weight into micro (250 g or less), very small (over 250 g to 2 kg), small (over 2 kg to 25 kg) and medium (over 25 kg to 150 kg), and a qualification or accreditation may be needed depending on the weight. Drones over 25 kg need approval even for recreational flying.

Before each flight, CASA recommends checking a CASA-verified drone safety app, which shows airspace restrictions and local rules. Approval may be needed in national parks, wildlife zones or on some private property, and rules vary by state and territory.
highlights: Recreational flying does not require registration, a licence or operator accreditation, including for micro drones. Flying for work or business requires drone registration plus operator accreditation or a remote pilot licence.

Fly at or below 120 m above ground level, and keep the drone in view with your own eyes, not through a screen, device or goggles. Do not fly through cloud, fog or smoke. Fly only in daylight and only one drone at a time.
Keep at least 30 m from other people and never fly over anyone. Do not fly in populated areas such as beaches, parks, events or sports ovals during games.

Near airports with a control tower, drones over 250 g must not fly within 5.5 km. Drones of 250 g or less may fly up to 45 m within 5.5 km, but not inside the airport boundary or in approach and departure paths. Near smaller airports without a control tower, flying within 5.5 km is permitted, but if you become aware of a crewed aircraft, do not launch, or move clear and land as soon as possible. The same applies within 1.4 km of helicopter landing sites.

Stay away from areas affecting public safety or emergency operations, such as police, search and rescue or firefighting, and respect other people's privacy. Approval may be needed in national parks, wildlife zones or on some private property.
checklist: Check your location in a CASA-verified drone safety app before every flight, and note the local rules it shows.
Check whether the place needs approval, such as national parks, wildlife zones and some private property, because rules vary by state and territory.
If the flight is for work or business, check CASA's pages on registration and on operator accreditation or a remote pilot licence before you fly.
Check the distance to airports (5.5 km) and helicopter landing sites (1.4 km), and keep clear of emergency operations.

ndFilter.metaTitle: Drone ND Filter Calculator – Pick the Right ND Strength
ndFilter.metaDescription: Enter your shutter speed and frame rate (180-degree rule) or a target shutter to get the ND strength you need and the resulting shutter.
ndFilter.title: Drone ND Filter Calculator
ndFilter.subtitle: Enter the shutter speed your camera picks without a filter and the shutter you want. We show the stops of light to cut and the closest ND filter.
ndFilter.baseShutterHelp: Use the value your drone app picks in auto exposure. Example: 1/1000 or 0.001
ndFilter.angleHelp: 180° gives the most natural motion blur. Target shutter = angle ÷ (360 × fps).
ndFilter.targetHelp: Enter a fraction (1/4) or seconds as a number (0.25, 2, 30).
ndFilter.invalid: Please enter valid values (shutter must be greater than 0).
ndFilter.noFilter: No ND filter needed. Your current shutter is already equal to or slower than the target.
ndFilter.exceeds: The reduction needed is beyond ND1000 (about 10 stops). Stacking filters can cause vignetting, so shoot in dimmer light or choose a faster target shutter.
ndFilter.tableCaption: Shutter speed with each filter, based on a current shutter of {shutter}
howToSteps: Before fitting a filter, read the shutter speed your drone app picks in auto exposure.
For video choose your frame rate (for example 30 fps); for photos or long exposures enter the shutter you want.
Fit the recommended filter and check the shutter shown on screen. If the light changes, move one step up or down.
For video, lock the shutter (manual exposure) and adjust brightness with ISO so motion blur stays consistent.
formulaBody: An ND filter of N stops cuts the light to 1 ÷ 2^N. To keep the same brightness the shutter must be 2^N times longer, so the stops needed are log₂(target shutter ÷ current shutter).
The 180-degree rule sets the shutter to half the frame interval: 1 ÷ (2 × fps). At 30 fps that is 1/60 s; at 60 fps, 1/120 s. ND4 is 2 stops, ND8 is 3 stops … ND1000 is about 10 stops (2¹⁰ = 1024).

faq.q: Does a bigger ND number mean darker?
faq.a: Yes. ND8 cuts light to 1/8 (3 stops) and ND64 to 1/64 (6 stops). Every time the number multiplies by 2 you lose one more stop.

faq.q: The shutter on screen differs slightly from the result.
faq.a: Standard ND filters come in whole stops, so a small gap is normal. Check the difference in the result card, pick the closest filter and fine-tune with ISO.

faq.q: Can I stack several ND filters?
faq.a: Stops add up (ND8 + ND16 = 7 stops), but image quality drops and vignetting risk rises with every extra filter. Use a single filter when you can.

faq.q: Do I need ND filters for photos too?
faq.a: They help for long-exposure shots in daylight, such as smooth water or streaking clouds. Use the photo / long exposure mode and enter your target shutter.

flightTime.shareText: Base {base} · wind {wind} m/s · {temp}°C → estimated flight time {total} ({usable} usable after reserve)
flightTime.metaTitle: Drone Flight Time Calculator – Wind and Cold Adjusted
flightTime.metaDescription: Start from rated flight time or battery specs, add wind, temperature, flying style and battery health, and estimate usable time and a safe turnaround.
flightTime.title: Drone Flight Time Calculator
flightTime.subtitle: Start from the rated flight time (or battery specs) and factor in wind, temperature and flying style to estimate how long you can really fly and when to head back.
flightTime.baseModeLabel: How to get the base time
flightTime.ratedHelp: The maximum flight time published by the manufacturer. Example: 34
flightTime.voltsHelp: The nominal voltage on the battery label. Example: 7.7, 11.4, 15.4
flightTime.weightHelp: Aircraft, battery and any accessories combined.
flightTime.powerHelp: Power needed to hold 1 kg in the air. Omni Calculator uses 170 by default (120 for a lower case). It varies by aircraft.
flightTime.healthHelp: 100 for a new battery; 80–90 if it has seen a lot of use.
flightTime.reserveHelp: Assumes you land with this much charge left. Landing with 20–30% left is a common safe margin.
flightTime.speedHelp: If entered, the maximum out-and-back radius is calculated too.
flightTime.invalid: Please enter valid values (all numbers must be greater than 0 and not empty).
flightTime.turnaroundHelp: Start heading back once this much time has passed.
flightTime.tableNote: These are rule-of-thumb assumptions, not manufacturer figures; values between rows are interpolated. Real numbers differ by aircraft and battery.
flightTime.warnWind: Wind of 10 m/s or more can be close to or beyond the wind resistance of many small drones. Check your manual's limit and don't fly if unsure.
flightTime.warnCold: Below 5°C, keep the battery warm until takeoff and hover briefly after launch. Low-voltage warnings may appear earlier than calculated.
flightTime.warnHot: Above 35°C, watch battery and electronics temperature. Overheating safety matters more than flight time.
howToSteps: Choose the base time. If you know the rated flight time, enter it; otherwise pick the battery-specs method and enter capacity, voltage and weight.
Enter the wind speed and temperature for your flight area, your flying style and the battery's health. You can check wind and temperature on the FlyDroneMap dashboard.
Read the estimated total flight time and the usable time after the landing reserve.
For out-and-back flights, start returning at the turnaround point, and earlier if part of the way back is into the wind.
formulaBody: Estimated total time = base time × flying-style factor × wind factor × temperature factor × battery health. Usable time subtracts the landing reserve, and the out-and-back turnaround is half of the usable time.

In the battery-specs method the base time is the ideal hover time: battery energy (Wh = Ah × V) times an 80% usable discharge, divided by power draw (weight × W/kg). Rated times are also measured in ideal conditions, so we apply the rule of thumb that typical shooting flights use about 75% of them (flying-style factor 0.75).

faq.q: Why is the result shorter than the manufacturer's number?
faq.a: Rated flight time is measured in ideal conditions with no wind and steady speed. In real flights wind, acceleration, temperature and battery age add up. This tool corrects for that to give a planning figure.

faq.q: Can't I fly the battery down to 0%?
faq.a: It is not recommended. The aircraft needs spare charge for low-battery warnings and automatic return, and in wind or cold the voltage can sag earlier than the displayed percentage suggests. Landing with 20–30% left is a common safety margin.

faq.q: How much does cold reduce flight time?
faq.a: Manufacturers don't publish a percentage; they only say capacity drops significantly. This tool assumes a 15–25% reduction around 0–5°C as a planning value. Check real behavior on a short first flight and adjust.

faq.q: Can I trust the result as-is?
faq.a: No. It is a planning estimate only. The aircraft's remaining-charge display, low-battery warnings and return-to-home settings always come first, and you should keep extra margin at unfamiliar sites.

batteryCheck.subtitle: Convert battery capacity (mAh) and voltage to watt-hours and see which airline carry-on class each battery falls into.
batteryCheck.voltsHelp: The nominal voltage on the battery label.
batteryCheck.whHelp: The Wh rating printed on the battery label.
batteryCheck.invalid: Please enter valid values (capacity, voltage and quantity must be numbers greater than 0).
batteryCheck.descStandard: Falls in the standard carry-on class. Spare batteries must travel in carry-on, not checked baggage, and quantity limits vary by airline.
batteryCheck.descApproval: Airline approval is required. Spare batteries are limited to two per person and must travel in carry-on.
batteryCheck.descForbidden: This capacity cannot be carried on a passenger aircraft.
batteryCheck.warnApprovalQty: You have {count} batteries in the approval range (100–160 Wh). Two per person is the usual limit, so check with your airline first.
batteryCheck.warnForbidden: One or more batteries exceed 160 Wh and cannot be carried as passenger baggage.
batteryCheck.protectBody: Cover the battery terminals (+/−) with insulating tape, or keep each battery in a battery case, protective pouch or its original packaging.
batteryCheck.installedNote: How the rules apply to a battery left installed in the aircraft can differ by airline, so check with your airline before flying.
batteryCheck.sourceIata: IATA – Passengers travelling with lithium batteries (PDF)
batteryCheck.verified: Checked against FAA and IATA passenger guidance as of November 2026. Rules can change and differ by country and airline, so confirm with your airline before you travel.
howToSteps: Find the Wh rating on the battery label. If it is there, pick "Wh printed on the label" and enter it.
If there is no Wh, enter capacity (mAh) and voltage (V). If you carry batteries of different capacities, add them as separate types.
Check each battery's class (up to 100 Wh / 100–160 Wh / over 160 Wh) and the total quantity.
Before you travel, read your airline's lithium battery guidance, insulate the terminals and carry the batteries in the cabin.
formulaBody: Wh = voltage (V) × capacity (Ah), and mAh is divided by 1000 to get Ah. For example a 5000 mAh, 15.4 V battery is 5 × 15.4 = 77 Wh. FAA and IATA both give this same formula.

The classes follow FAA and IATA passenger guidance: up to 100 Wh is standard carry-on, over 100 Wh up to 160 Wh needs airline approval (two spares per person), and over 160 Wh cannot go on a passenger aircraft. Spare batteries must always travel in the cabin.

faq.q: My battery has no Wh printed on it.
faq.a: Calculate it from the label's voltage (V) and capacity (mAh): Wh = V × mAh ÷ 1000. Example: 5000 mAh × 15.4 V ÷ 1000 = 77 Wh. Lithium-ion batteries normally carry a Wh rating, so look at the label first.

faq.q: Can I put drone batteries in checked baggage?
faq.a: FAA and IATA both say spare (loose) lithium batteries must be carried in carry-on baggage, not checked baggage. The same applies to drone batteries.

faq.q: Can't I take a battery over 100 Wh?
faq.a: Over 100 Wh up to 160 Wh can go in the cabin with airline approval, limited to two spares per person. Anything over 160 Wh cannot be carried on a passenger aircraft.

faq.q: Are the rules the same as for power banks?
faq.a: No. Power banks are seeing separate, stricter airline limits on quantity and use. Treat drone batteries under the spare-battery rules above, and check your airline's latest guidance.

goldenHour.polarNight: At this location the sun does not rise on this date (polar night), so there is no sunrise or sunset time.
goldenHour.droneBody: Flying before sunrise or after sunset is treated differently by country and region. Check night-flight permission, lighting requirements and visibility conditions on our regulations page and with your local aviation authority.
goldenHour.serverNote: Only the place-name search goes through our server; the sun calculation from coordinates and date runs in your browser.
howToSteps: Search for a city or place and pick a result, or use "Use my location" or enter coordinates manually.
Choose a date. It defaults to today and you can change it to your planned shoot day.
Read the sunrise and sunset times and directions, and the morning and evening golden hour and blue hour windows.
Arrive at least 30 minutes early to check the aircraft and batteries, and look at weather and KP index on the dashboard.
formulaBody: The tool uses the NOAA solar position algorithm to get the sun's elevation and azimuth for a date and place, then scans the day minute by minute for the moments the sun crosses each reference elevation. Sunrise and sunset use −0.833° (refraction and the sun's radius).

Golden hour is calculated as a solar elevation of about −4° to +6°, and blue hour as about −8° to −4°. These are common photographic conventions and sources differ slightly. Terrain, buildings and cloud change the real light.

faq.q: When is golden hour?
faq.a: It is the period just after sunrise and just before sunset when the sun is low and the light is soft and warm. Its length depends on location and season, so enter your place and date above to get the exact times.

faq.q: How is blue hour different from golden hour?
faq.a: Blue hour is the bluish twilight just after sunset (or before sunrise). The sky is still bright while city lights come on, which suits cityscape shots. Night-flight rules differ by country, so check them first.

faq.q: The times differ by a minute or two from another app.
faq.a: Differences of a minute or two can come from the reference elevation (refraction) and whether terrain elevation is included. Near mountains the time you actually see sunlight can be earlier or later than calculated.

faq.q: No times appear at high latitudes.
faq.a: In summer the sun may not set (midnight sun) and in winter it may not rise (polar night), so there is no sunrise or sunset. In that case you get a note plus the day timeline showing how the light changes.

gsd.metaTitle: Drone GSD Calculator – Ground Resolution by Altitude
gsd.metaDescription: Find a drone photo's GSD (cm per pixel), ground footprint and shot spacing from altitude, sensor and focal length, or the altitude for a target GSD.
gsd.title: Drone GSD Calculator
gsd.subtitle: From your altitude and camera specs, find how much ground one pixel covers (GSD), the footprint of each photo and the shot spacing for your overlap.
gsd.focalHelp: The lens's real focal length, not the 35 mm equivalent. Use the "actual" value from the spec sheet.
gsd.speedHelp: Enter it to also get the shot interval in seconds.
gsd.invalid: Please enter valid values (every field must be a number greater than 0).
gsd.invalidOverlap: Enter overlap values from 0 up to less than 100.
gsd.warnAltitude: The altitude is above about 120 m (400 ft). Many regions cap flight height at that level, so check local rules or consider a longer lens or a higher-resolution camera.
gsd.orientationNote: Assumes the image's short side points along the flight direction. If you shoot with the camera rotated 90 degrees, swap width and height.
howToSteps: Choose "Altitude → GSD" and enter your altitude, or choose "Target GSD → altitude" and enter the resolution you want.
Tap a sensor format or type the sensor size, then enter the lens's actual focal length and the image size in pixels.
Set forward and side overlap to get the distance between shots and the flight line spacing. Add a speed to get the shot interval in seconds.
Check that the resulting altitude is within your local maximum flight height, and adjust the target or camera if needed.
formulaBody: GSD (cm/pixel) = altitude (m) × sensor width (mm) ÷ (focal length (mm) × image width in pixels) × 100. For example a 1-inch sensor (13.2 mm), 10.3 mm lens and 5472 pixels flown at 100 m gives about 2.3 cm/pixel.

The footprint is GSD times the pixel count. Distance between shots is footprint length × (1 − forward overlap) and line spacing is footprint width × (1 − side overlap). Sensor sizes are typical values per format and can differ slightly from the manufacturer's spec.

faq.q: Is a smaller GSD always better?
faq.a: A smaller GSD means each pixel covers less ground, so you see more detail. But covering the same area needs a lower altitude and more photos, which costs flight time and battery. Choose only as fine as your purpose needs.

faq.q: Which focal length should I enter?
faq.a: Enter the lens's actual focal length (for example 10.3 mm), not the 35 mm equivalent. If you only know the equivalent, divide it by the crop factor to get the actual value.

faq.q: How much overlap is enough?
faq.a: For mapping, about 70–80% forward and 60–70% side overlap is common. Low-texture ground such as forest or water usually calls for more.

faq.q: Does this guarantee survey accuracy?
faq.a: No. It is a theoretical figure for photo resolution. Real survey accuracy depends on ground control, position correction, lens distortion correction and terrain relief.

densityAltitude.metaTitle: Drone Density Altitude Calculator – Hot & High Flying
densityAltitude.metaDescription: Calculate density altitude, air density ratio and extra hover power from elevation, temperature and QNH to judge drone performance when hot or high.
densityAltitude.title: Drone Density Altitude Calculator
densityAltitude.subtitle: From elevation, temperature and pressure, see how thin the air really is (density altitude) and how much more power a hover takes.
densityAltitude.elevationHelp: Height above sea level. The elevation shown in a map app is fine.
densityAltitude.qnhHelp: The sea-level pressure (QNH) from a weather app. Standard is 1013 hPa (29.92 inHg).
densityAltitude.invalid: Please enter valid values (elevation −1,500 to 30,000 ft, temperature −60 to 60 °C, pressure 850–1090 hPa).
densityAltitude.hoverPowerSub: Theoretical extra power versus standard air
densityAltitude.isaLine: Standard temperature at this altitude is {isa}{unit}; today is {dev}{unit} from standard.
densityAltitude.levelSmall: Density altitude is close to your real elevation, so expect near-normal performance.
densityAltitude.levelNoticeable: The air is noticeably thinner than standard. Propeller efficiency and climb rate drop and motors work harder, so plan battery margins generously.
densityAltitude.levelLarge: The air is much thinner. Climb and hover performance can fall sharply and motors and batteries run hotter. Reduce payload and check the manufacturer's maximum operating altitude and temperature.
howToSteps: Pick your units and enter the takeoff site's elevation above sea level.
Enter the air temperature. Midday ground temperature is the worst case, so use the forecast for your flight time.
Enter the sea-level pressure (QNH) from a weather app or airport report. Leave the standard value if you do not know it.
Read the density altitude and hover power change. If they are large, re-check payload, flight time and operating limits.
formulaBody: Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013.25 − QNH) × 27 ft, and the standard temperature is 15 °C − 1.98 °C per 1,000 ft of pressure altitude. Density altitude is approximated as pressure altitude + 118.8 × (actual − standard temperature) ft, while the air density ratio comes from the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) model.

Hover power is assumed to scale with the inverse square root of the air density ratio (a theoretical figure). Humidity is not included, so on a humid day the air is a little thinner than shown. Real performance varies by aircraft, so follow the manufacturer's specifications first.

faq.q: What is density altitude?
faq.a: It restates today's air density as the altitude where standard air has the same density. Heat, low pressure and high ground all raise it, and the propellers then produce less lift.

faq.q: Does it matter at sea level on a summer afternoon?
faq.a: Yes. Even at sea level, air 15–20 °C above the 15 °C standard raises density altitude by roughly 1,500–2,000 ft. In heat, also check battery performance and temperature.

faq.q: Is the hover power change exact?
faq.a: No, it is a rough theoretical figure. Propeller design, speed and payload change the real result, so use it only as a comparison.

faq.q: What if I do not know the QNH?
faq.a: Leaving the standard 1013 hPa (29.92 inHg) still gives a rough result. For better accuracy, enter the sea-level pressure from a weather app.

lineOfSight.shareText: {kind, select, distance {Pilot eye height {pilot} · drone altitude {altitude} → visual horizon {geo}, radio range {radio}} other {Pilot eye height {pilot} · target distance {distance} → required altitude {geo} (visual), {radio} (radio)}}
lineOfSight.metaDescription: Find the horizon distance and radio line-of-sight range from drone altitude and pilot eye height, or the altitude needed for a target distance.
lineOfSight.title: Drone Line-of-Sight & Radio Horizon Calculator
lineOfSight.subtitle: From flight altitude and pilot position, find how far the horizon is given the Earth's curvature and the theoretical range a radio link can reach.
lineOfSight.altitudeHelp: Height of the drone above the ground, not above the pilot.
lineOfSight.pilotHelp: About 1.6 m standing on flat ground; add the height if you are on a hill or building.
lineOfSight.invalid: Please enter valid values (altitude and distance must be greater than 0, eye height 0 or more).
lineOfSight.geoDistanceSub: Where the Earth's curvature hides the drone below the horizon (ignoring atmospheric refraction)
lineOfSight.radioDistanceSub: Standard model with atmospheric refraction (4/3 Earth), about 15% farther
lineOfSight.pilotHorizonSub: Distance to the horizon from the pilot's eye height alone
lineOfSight.geoAltitudeSub: Minimum height for the drone to sit above the horizon at the target distance
lineOfSight.radioAltitudeSub: Minimum height for a straight radio path at the target distance
lineOfSight.vlosNote: These figures consider Earth's curvature only. Trees, buildings, terrain, interference and transmit power are not included, and in most countries you must keep the drone within visual line of sight (VLOS). The distance at which you can actually see a small drone is far shorter.
howToSteps: Choose a mode: "Altitude → range" to see the reach from a height, or "Distance → required altitude" to see the height needed for a distance.
Enter the drone's altitude (or the target distance).
Enter the pilot's eye height. Add the height of any hill or building you stand on.
Compare the visual and radio ranges, and plan the actual flight within visual line of sight and your local maximum altitude.
formulaBody: With Earth radius R = 6,371 km, the horizon from height h (m) is √(2·R·h). Adding the horizon distances of the pilot and the drone gives the greatest distance at which the two can be joined by a straight line. A drone at 120 m with a pilot eye height of 1.6 m gives roughly 39–40 km.

Radio waves bend slightly with the atmosphere, so the standard model uses 4/3 of the Earth's radius, which lengthens the distance by about 15%. This is an upper bound with no obstacles at all; real video-link range is usually far shorter because of interference, power, antennas and terrain.

faq.q: Can I fly out to the calculated distance?
faq.a: No. The figure is a theoretical limit based on Earth's curvature alone. In most countries you must keep the drone in visual line of sight (VLOS), and a small drone is usually only recognizable by eye at a few hundred metres.

faq.q: Why is the radio range longer than the visual horizon?
faq.a: Air density changes with height, which bends radio waves slightly along the surface. The standard model treats the Earth as 4/3 of its radius, so the horizon is about 15% farther.

faq.q: How much does more altitude extend the range?
faq.a: Distance scales with the square root of height, so quadrupling altitude doubles the horizon distance. But regulations cap altitude (for example 120 m), so check local rules first.

faq.q: Are transmit power and antennas included?
faq.a: No. This calculator shows only the geometric limit. Actual range depends on power, antennas, the radio environment and obstacles.

checklist.metaTitle: Drone Preflight Checklist – Check Off and Print
checklist.metaDescription: Drone preflight checklist covering rules, weather, aircraft, batteries, takeoff site and in-flight checks. Tick items off and print it for the field.
checklist.title: Drone Preflight Checklist
checklist.subtitle: Run through rules, weather, aircraft, batteries and the takeoff site in one place before every flight, and print it if you want a paper copy.
checklist.allDone: Every item is checked. Take one last look at local rules and the aircraft, then fly safely.
checklist.storageNote: Your ticks are saved only in this browser and never sent to a server. Use Reset to clear them at any time.

groups.title: 1. Rules and permissions
items: I checked that the site is not a no-fly or restricted zone (airports, military sites, parks, events)
Any required authorization is in hand and has not expired
Aircraft and operator registration and insurance are valid
I know the maximum altitude (e.g. 120 m) and the visual line of sight (VLOS) rules
I know the required distances from people, vehicles and buildings
I checked privacy and local filming rules for any recording

groups.title: 2. Weather and environment
items: I checked wind and gust forecasts for my flight window (within the aircraft's limit)
I checked precipitation and visibility (rain, snow, fog)
Temperature is within the battery's recommended range (not too cold or hot)
I checked the Kp index and GPS satellite status
I checked sunrise and sunset and set a time to finish

groups.title: 3. Aircraft
items: Propellers have no cracks, bends or chips and are firmly mounted
Frame, arms and folding joints show no damage or looseness
Motors spin smoothly without binding or debris
Gimbal cover is removed and the lens is clean
Vision sensors (forward and downward) are clean
Firmware and app are up to date with no warnings

groups.title: 4. Batteries and controller
items: The flight battery is fully charged and not swollen or damaged
Controller and phone or tablet have enough charge
A memory card is inserted with enough free space
Spare batteries and propellers are packed
The controller link and video feed are working

groups.title: 5. Takeoff site
items: The takeoff spot is flat, firm and clear of obstacles
I checked overhead trees, wires and buildings
No people, animals or vehicles are close by
I avoided magnetic interference (steel structures, power equipment, buried metal)
The home point is recorded correctly and return altitude clears nearby obstacles

groups.title: 6. Just after takeoff and in flight
items: I hovered at 1–2 m to check control response and unusual vibration
I keep watching battery level and the margin needed to return
I keep the aircraft in sight and know its position and heading
I know the emergency steps to land or return immediately if something goes wrong

howToSteps: Go through the items from the top before you fly, tapping each one to tick it off.
Items that do not apply can be left or ticked as you like; the progress count is only a guide.
Press Print if you want a paper copy to use in the field.
After the flight, press Reset to clear the ticks and reuse the list next time.
formulaBody: The checklist follows the order of a flight: rules, weather, aircraft, batteries, takeoff site, then flight. Check the rules before choosing a site, and look at the aircraft and the takeoff area once you arrive.

It is a reference list of general safety practice and does not cover every situation. The manufacturer's manual and your local aviation authority's rules always come first. Add or skip items to suit your own flying.

faq.q: How were the items chosen?
faq.a: They are the rules, weather, aircraft, battery, takeoff-site and in-flight checks beginners most often miss, drawn from general safety practice. They do not replace the manufacturer's manual or local rules.

faq.q: Where are my ticks stored?
faq.a: Only in this device's browser. Nothing is sent to a server, and clearing browser data or pressing Reset removes them.

faq.q: Do the ticks appear when I print?
faq.a: Yes, the page prints as it currently looks. To print a blank list, press Reset first.

faq.q: Can I add my own items?
faq.a: Not at the moment; the list is fixed. We suggest writing any extra items on the printed copy.

euCategory.metaTitle: EU Drone Class (C0–C4) & A1/A2/A3 Subcategory Checker
euCategory.metaDescription: Pick your drone's C-class label and weight to see its EU open-category subcategory (A1, A2, A3), training, registration and Remote ID.
euCategory.title: EU Drone Class & Subcategory Checker
euCategory.subtitle: Choose your drone's class label (C0–C4) and weight to see which EU open-category subcategory (A1, A2, A3) applies, and what training and registration you need.
euCategory.classHelp_C0: A drone carrying the C0 label, under 250 g. Most small camera drones fall here.
euCategory.classHelp_C1: A drone carrying the C1 label, under 900 g, with built-in Remote ID.
euCategory.classHelp_C2: A drone carrying the C2 label, under 4 kg. It can be flown closer to people in subcategory A2.
euCategory.classHelp_C3: A drone carrying the C3 label, under 25 kg. It is flown only in A3, away from people.
euCategory.classHelp_C4: A drone carrying the C4 label, under 25 kg, mostly model-aircraft types, flown in A3.
euCategory.classHelp_legacy: A drone without a class label that was placed on the market before 1 January 2024. Unlabelled drones sold after that date fall in the specific category.
euCategory.classHelp_private: A drone you built yourself. Enter its take-off mass.
euCategory.classHelp_C5C6: Drones with a C5 or C6 label are for the specific category only.
euCategory.massHelp: Enter the maximum take-off mass (MTOM) from the spec sheet, including camera and battery.
euCategory.cameraLabel: Does it have a camera or data-gathering sensor?
euCategory.invalidMass: Enter the take-off mass in grams as a number greater than 0.
euCategory.tooHeavy: 25 kg or more is outside the open category. The specific category, which needs operational authorisation, applies.
euCategory.specific: C5 and C6 drones can only be flown in the specific category, which needs an operational authorisation or standard scenario procedure.
euCategory.sub_A1_rule: You may fly close to people but never over assemblies of people, and you should avoid flying over uninvolved people.
euCategory.sub_A2_rule: Keep 30 m horizontally from uninvolved people (reducible to 5 m in a C2 low-speed mode).
euCategory.sub_A3_rule: Fly at least 150 m from residential, commercial, industrial or recreational areas, where no uninvolved people are at risk.
euCategory.training_a1a3: Pass the A1/A3 online training and exam.
euCategory.training_a2: A1/A3 training, plus practical self-training and the A2 exam (A2 certificate).
euCategory.training_none: No remote pilot certificate is required (check national rules).
euCategory.registration_ifCamera_yes: Required because it has a camera or sensor (unless it is a toy).
euCategory.registration_ifCamera_no: Usually not required for a drone under 250 g without a camera or sensor.
euCategory.remoteId_required: Direct Remote ID must be built into the drone.
euCategory.remoteId_check: Direct Remote ID is not required by this class. Check your country's requirements.
euCategory.legacyNote: Drones without a label follow the transitional rules based on when they were placed on the market. Under 250 g they fly in A1 (A3 also allowed); from 250 g to under 25 kg only in A3. No sticker is needed.
euCategory.generalLimits: Open category basics: keep visual line of sight (some exceptions), fly at most 120 m above ground, carry no dangerous goods and drop nothing, never fly over assemblies of people, and keep the drone under 25 kg.
euCategory.nationalNote: Minimum age, insurance and registration details differ by country and extra rules may apply. Check your national aviation authority before flying.
euCategory.verified: Cross-checked against official EASA, German and Spanish guidance in November 2026. Rules can change, so check the latest guidance before you fly.
howToSteps: Find the class label (C0–C4) on your drone and pick the same option. With no label, choose "No class label" or "Privately built".
For an unlabelled or home-built drone, enter its maximum take-off mass in grams.
For drones under 250 g, say whether it has a camera or sensor.
Read the subcategories, training, registration and Remote ID in the result, then confirm the latest rules through the official links.
formulaBody: The EU open category divides flying by the drone's class label and mass. C0 (under 250 g) and C1 (under 900 g) fly in A1 and A3, C2 (under 4 kg) in A2 and A3, and C3 and C4 (under 25 kg) in A3. C5 and C6 are for the specific category only.

Existing drones without a label are sorted by weight: under 250 g in A1 (A3 included), 250 g to under 25 kg in A3, and 25 kg or more falls outside the open category. This checker summarises the key points of official guidance such as EASA's; it is a reference, not legal advice.

faq.q: Where do I find the class label?
faq.a: Drones sold in the EU from 2024 carry a C0–C4 label on the aircraft and its packaging. It also appears in the user manual and the manufacturer's declaration of conformity.

faq.q: Are drones under 250 g free of rules?
faq.a: No. Even under 250 g, a drone with a camera or sensor (other than a toy) needs operator registration, and the open-category basics, such as the 120 m limit and no flights over assemblies of people, plus national rules still apply.

faq.q: When is A2 used?
faq.a: When you want to fly a C2 drone closer to people (30 m horizontally, 5 m in low-speed mode). It needs an A2 certificate, which involves training and an exam.

faq.q: Does this apply outside the EU?
faq.a: These rules apply in EU member states, and some other European countries use similar frameworks. The UK and other countries have their own rules, so check the national aviation authority.
